newsitem.title: CANADA: Germany disallows Potash Corp.'s Kali deal.
newsitem.headline: Germany disallows Potash Corp.'s Kali deal.

text.p: A German government minister on Tuesday blocked Potash Corp. of Saskatchewan Inc.'s yearlong bid to acquire a German fertiliser producer from BASF AG, in a move analysts said may have sealed the deal's demise.

The decision by German Economics Minister Guenter Rexrodt to disallow Potash Corp.'s $139 million acquisition of 51 percent of Kali & Salz sent the Saskatoon, Saskatchewan-based fertiliser producer's stock tumbling in Toronto and New York.

PCS Vice President Betty-Ann Heggie said in a telephone interview that the company's lawyers were reviewing the decision and would recommend whether to launch a court appeal in Germany within the next 30 days.
"We've put a lot of time and energy into this, so it's obviously disappointing," Heggie said.

The company's shares on the Toronto Stock Exchange were down C$4.45 to C$103.55 in early afternoon trading. PCS fell $2.56 to $75.56 in consolidated trading on the New York Stock Exchange. PCS announced the deal last August with hopes of gaining
control over 18 percent of the world's potash production and opening new distribution lines in Europe.

Kali & Salz is Germany's biggest producer of potash, one of three nutrients used to make agricultural fertilisers. The remaining 49 percent of the company is owned by east German development agency BvS.
PCS, the world's largest potash company, is also a leader in the production of nitrogen and phosphate after billions of dollars worth of acquisitions over the past three years.
The Canadian company and BASF said late last year they struck a definitive sale agreement.
But Germany's Cartel Office in February said it would not allow the deal, citing a possible dominance of the German potash market.
Potash and BASF then appealed to Rexrodt, who decided after a series of public hearings that the deal could reduce competition in the country's fertiliser industry.
"An obvious and concrete danger of anti-competition does not serve the public interest. Because of this, I did not give my permission for the sale," he said.
Heggie said the decision was made despite backing for the deal from PCS, Kali & Salz, BASF, unions representing the target's workers and politicians in mining areas.

PCS's offer was the best option for retaining 7,500 jobs at Kali & Salz, and the government move placed them at jeopardy, Gerhard Wolf, the BASF board member responsible for the fertiliser firm, said in Ludwigshafen, Germany.

Sam Kanes, an analyst with Scotia Capital Markets in Toronto, said investors should have factored the risk of the deal not being completed into their outlooks for PCS, given the previous disapprovals.
Kanes said he believed the company would probably not take the issue further.
"They've gone through a monopoly and a cartel 'no' ruling and now, of course, the economics minister, which carries the most amount of weight, said 'no' as well," he said.
"The German government has spoken. Going through the courts is just going to antagonize people."
PCS planned to keep evaluating new acquisitions regardless of the outcome of the Kali & Salz deal's outcome, Heggie said.
